title: Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare

definition.text: The Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW) is an economic indicator proposed as a replacement for GDP, the main headline figure of national accounts.

facts.text: Instead of just adding up spending, the ISEW weighs consumer spending against income distribution and the costs of pollution and other unsustainable practices.

Its rough formula: personal consumption plus public non-defensive spending, minus private defensive spending, plus capital formation and household labour services, minus environmental degradation costs and natural capital depreciation.
Ecological economist Herman Daly and theologian John B. Cobb developed the ISEW in 1989 as a more valid measure of progress than GDP.
Cobb and Daly's US calculation for 1950 to 1986 found average economic welfare levelled off after the 1970s even as GDP kept growing.
They blamed the side effects of production and unequal income distribution for production gains not turning into welfare gains.
The ISEW has also been compiled for many other places, including the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Chile, Finland, Poland, Belgium, Pakistan and China.
Like GDP, the ISEW boils welfare down to one number, but it puts social and environmental issues into the sum in money terms.

title: Genuine progress indicator

definition.text: The genuine progress indicator (GPI) is a measure proposed to replace or supplement GDP by counting environmental and social factors that GDP leaves out.

facts.text: GDP counts pollution twice as a gain, once when it is made and again when it is cleaned up; the GPI instead counts it as a loss, roughly equal to its clean-up and damage costs.
In simplified form GPI = A + B - C - D + I: income-weighted consumption plus non-market services, minus defensive costs and nature's deterioration, plus capital growth and trade balance.
The GPI rests on John Hicks's idea of sustainable income: what can be consumed in one period without reducing consumption in the next.
It is built from 26 indicators grouped into economic, environmental and social categories.
The GPI grew out of later work extending the ISEW, with extra emphasis on welfare and the ecological sustainability of the economy.
As of 2014, Vermont, Maryland, Washington and Hawaii had passed state initiatives to consider the GPI in budgeting.
Statistics Finland's series from 1945 to 2011 showed GDP and GPI rising together in the 1970s and 1980s, then diverging after the early-1990s recession.
Critics say GPI is harder to measure than GDP, depends on a contested definition of well-being, and is more open to political manipulation.

contested_note: Whether money growth reflects lost well-being is called a main issue between green and neoclassical economists, and critics question whether GPI can be defined or measured objectively.

title: Human Development Index

definition.text: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite score of life expectancy, schooling and income per person, used to rank countries into four tiers of human development.

facts.text: Economist Mahbub ul-Haq created it, and the UN Development Programme's Human Development Report Office uses it to measure countries' development.
The reports, launched in 1990, aimed to move development economics away from national income accounting towards people-centred policies.
It rests on Amartya Sen's capability idea: whether people are able to 'be' and 'do' desirable things, such as being healthy or taking part in community life.
Since 2010 it combines life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and gross national income per person at purchasing power parity.
Each dimension is scaled to an index between 0 and 1, and the HDI is the geometric mean of the three.
The 2010 report added an inequality-adjusted HDI, seen as the actual level of human development, while the plain HDI shows the potential with no inequality.
Critics point to its neglect of sustainability, inequality and democracy; a planetary pressures-adjusted HDI was later added to address sustainability.
One study found 11%, 21% and 34% of countries could be misclassified because of data updates, formula revisions and arbitrary thresholds respectively.

title: Measure of Economic Welfare

definition.text: The Measure of Economic Welfare (MEW), introduced by William Nordhaus and James Tobin in 1972, was the first model to estimate households' real yearly consumption as a welfare measure.

facts.text: Nordhaus and Tobin argued welfare must be sustainable, since nations that eat up their capital stock are less well off than national income suggests.
It belongs to a family of welfare indices, with Japan's Net National Welfare (1973) and the ISEW (1989), that add positive and negative nonmarket items to national accounts.
Clifford Cobb and John Cobb later argued the MEW failed to include the depletion of natural capital.

title: Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index

definition.text: The inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), introduced in the 2010 Human Development Report, discounts the HDI for inequality to show the actual level of human development.

facts.text: The plain HDI can be read as the potential, maximum human development a country could reach if there were no inequality.
The IHDI and the Gender Inequality Index were both adopted in 2010, growing out of the capability approach.

notes: Mentioned on Human Development Index and Capability approach pages.

title: Hicksian sustainable income

definition.text: Sustainable (Hicksian) income is the most a person or an economy can consume in one period without reducing what it can consume in the next.

facts.text: John Hicks (1946) said the practical point of measuring income is to show the most people can produce and consume without undermining their ability to do the same in future.
For a nation the question becomes whether its whole GDP can be consumed without harming its ability to produce the same GDP later, a question largely ignored in mainstream economics.
The genuine progress indicator is built on this idea, judging welfare by the ability to keep it at least as high in future.

title: Beyond GDP

definition.text: Beyond GDP is the push to develop broad measures of economic well-being that go further than GDP and other national income figures.

facts.text: Approaches include the European Union's Beyond GDP programme, the OECD's Better Lives indicators and many alternative measures of wellbeing or happiness.
Bhutan's Gross National Happiness Index was one of the earliest national attempts, and similar projects followed, such as the UK's measure of national well-being.
The European Commission sorts the alternatives into five groups: GDP itself, enlarged GDP measures, social indicators, environmental indicators and well-being measures.
Enlarged GDP measures subtract costs such as environmental degradation, resource depletion or higher income inequality.
Some proposals aim to replace GDP outright, while many others aim to supplement it with a 'dashboard' of metrics for the economy and well-being.
The World Bank suggests the HDI, Gross National Happiness and Adjusted Net Savings as alternatives to GDP.

title: Beyond GDP conference and EU actions
article: Broad measures of economic progress#Beyond GDP

definition.text: The 'Beyond GDP' conference of 2007, hosted by the European Commission, European Parliament, Club of Rome, OECD and WWF, sought wider measures of progress to guide policy.

facts.text: More than 650 policy makers, experts and social activists attended.
The EU communication 'GDP and beyond' set five actions, including complementing GDP with environmental and social indicators and extending national accounts to environmental and social issues.
Results included the EU's first quality-of-life indicators and backing for UN adoption of the System of Environmental Economic Accounting as the international standard.

title: UK Measuring National Well-being programme
article: Broad measures of economic progress#Measuring national well-being in the UK

definition.text: The Measuring National Well-being programme, launched in the UK in 2010 and led by the Office for National Statistics, aims to build trusted measures of the nation's well-being.

facts.text: Its well-being wheel has headline indicators for health, relationships, job satisfaction, economic security, education, environment and people's own rating of their well-being.
It has published experimental work such as household satellite accounts that value unpaid household production.

title: Green gross domestic product

definition.text: Green GDP is a measure of economic growth that subtracts the environmental consequences of that growth from a country's ordinary GDP.

facts.text: In simple form, green GDP equals GDP minus environmental costs minus social costs.
Environmental costs include depletion of resources such as oil and timber, ecological damage such as topsoil erosion, and restoration costs such as wetland restoration.
The motive is that GDP measures output alone and ignores the depletion or replenishment of the assets behind it, so it cannot tell if income is sustainable.
Benefits from forests, wetlands and farmland stay hidden in GDP because they are hard to measure and price.
Early work came from Nordhaus and Tobin (1972), Ahmad et al. (1989), Repetto et al. (1989) and Hartwick (1990).
The UN's environmental accounting system (SEEA) makes it possible to build full accounts from which green GDP can be derived and compared between countries.
In the US, early green accounts in 1994 showed GDP overstated mining's contribution to national wealth, and a 1995 amendment halted the work.
Critics say non-market assets such as ecosystem services are hard to value, and Stiglitz, Sen and Fitoussi argued green GDP does not measure sustainability itself.

contested_note: Experts disagree on whether environmental adjustments should be made inside the existing national accounts or by redefining what counts as income, and whether non-market assets can be reliably valued.

title: Green GDP in China
article: Green gross domestic product#Green GDP in China

definition.text: China's green GDP experiment was a national attempt, announced in 2004, to replace GDP with green GDP as a performance measure for top officials.

facts.text: The first green GDP report, for 2004, put the financial loss from pollution at 511.8 billion yuan ($66.3 billion), or 3.05 percent of the economy.
The effort collapsed in 2007 when environmental adjustments cut growth to politically unacceptable levels, nearly zero in some provinces, and the 2005 report was suppressed.
Its failure is linked to a mismatch between central authorities and local governments.

notes: Country-specific case, kept as the best-known national green GDP experiment.

title: Inclusive wealth

definition.text: Inclusive wealth is the total value of all capital assets in a place, including human, social, public and natural capital.

facts.text: Unlike GDP, the Inclusive Wealth Index lets countries check whether they are developing in a way that lets future generations meet their own needs.
UNEP developed the index with Kyushu University; it estimates stocks of human, natural and produced capital, the productive base of an economy.
The change in wealth sums the changes in each capital stock, each weighted by its shadow price, the estimated price of something with no market price.
Natural capital includes renewable resources such as farmland, forests and fisheries and non-renewables such as fossil fuels and minerals.
Inclusive Wealth Reports were published in 2012, 2014 and 2018; the first was launched at the Rio+20 conference.
The 2018 report found inclusive wealth in 140 countries rose 44% from 1990 to 2014, about 1.8% a year.
Yet 44 of the 140 countries saw inclusive wealth per person fall since 1992 while GDP per person rose in nearly all, a sign of unsustainable resource depletion.
Globally, produced capital per person has grown most, often at the expense of natural capital.

contested_note: Using shadow prices for natural capital is called controversial because of gaps in knowing how life-supporting ecosystems produce value.

title: Wellbeing economy

definition.text: A wellbeing economy is a public policy framework in which the economy is designed to serve social, health, cultural, fairness and nature outcomes.

facts.text: Its aim is to move beyond GDP as the main measure of how well a national economy is doing.
Several countries use wellbeing metrics to guide policy and budgets, focusing on education and skills, health, gender and inclusion.
Scotland, New Zealand, Iceland, Wales, Finland and Canada adopted it as national policy and formed the Wellbeing Economy Governments partnership (WEGo) in 2021.
The World Health Organization has also adopted wellbeing as a whole-of-government approach, first set out in the 2021 Geneva Charter for Wellbeing.
The Wellbeing Economy Alliance, founded in 2018, is the leading network of organisations and movements working towards a wellbeing economy.
An Ipsos survey in 17 of the G20 countries found 68% of respondents supported putting wellbeing ahead of profit.
Wellbeing economics is grouped with doughnut economics, steady-state economics and degrowth under the umbrella of post-growth thinking.

title: New Zealand Wellbeing Budget

definition.text: New Zealand's Wellbeing Budget, launched in May 2019, was the country's first budget built around people's wellbeing and the environment rather than GDP alone.

facts.text: It chose five priorities: climate and environment, productive work, Maori and Pacific opportunities, child wellbeing, and mental and physical health.
Prime Minister Ardern argued citizens' health and life satisfaction, not wealth or growth, should be the measure of a country's progress.
The next, National-led coalition government dropped the approach in 2024.

notes: Country-specific, kept as the pioneering example of a wellbeing budget.

title: Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission
article: Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress

definition.text: The Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress, known as the Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission, was an inquiry set up by the French government in 2008.

facts.text: It examined how a nation's wealth and social progress could be measured without relying on the one-dimensional GDP figure.
Joseph Stiglitz chaired it, Amartya Sen was economic adviser and Jean-Paul Fitoussi coordinator; its final report came out in September 2009.
It proposed a well-being framework covering health, environment, work, physical safety, economic safety and political freedom.
Its report argued that green GDP and similar indices only charge GDP for environmental damage and do not measure sustainability as such.

title: Defensive expenditures

definition.text: In environmental accounting, defensive expenditures are spending meant to limit possible damage to oneself.

facts.text: Standard accounts do not subtract this spending to fight 'bads', so it counts as if it were a gain.
The ISEW subtracts private defensive spending and counts only non-defensive public spending.
GDP treats money spent repairing earlier harm, such as rebuilding destroyed homes, the same as money spent on new production.
Spending people make to protect themselves from pollution can also reveal how much they value avoiding it.

title: Green national product

definition.text: The green national product is a measure that folds environmental degradation and resource depletion into a country's national product.

facts.text: Critics say GNP puts the environment on the wrong side of the ledger: polluting and then cleaning up both add to GNP.
GNP lumps spending that makes people worse off, keeps them in place, or makes them better off into one figure, giving no clue about real progress.
Herman Daly argued GNP ignores a basic business accounting rule that all revenues and expenses are allocated to income.
The line of welfare adjustments runs from the MEW to the ISEW (1989) to the GPI (1995), which also adjusts for housework, volunteering, crime and leisure.

title: Gross National Happiness

definition.text: Gross National Happiness (GNH) is a philosophy followed by Bhutan's government, with an index measuring a population's collective happiness and well-being.

facts.text: Bhutan's 4th King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, coined it in 1972, declaring it more important than GDP.
Its four pillars are fair socio-economic development, environmental conservation, preserving culture and good governance, alongside nine domains including ecological diversity and resilience.
Each domain mixes survey-based and objective indicators, and people are classed as happy or not-yet-happy by their scores.
The GNH Index became Bhutan's official goal in its 2008 Constitution, and screening tools test new policies and projects against it.
In 2011 a UN General Assembly resolution urged members to follow Bhutan and measure happiness and well-being.
Versions of the GNH survey were used in places such as Victoria in Canada, Seattle and Vermont.
Critics call it a propaganda tool that distracted from Bhutan's expulsion of its Nepalese Hindu minority and from widespread poverty.

contested_note: Critics describe GNH as a government propaganda tool, while others see it as an evolving, more democratic development philosophy.

title: Happiness economics

definition.text: Happiness economics is the study of happiness, well-being, life satisfaction and quality of life, linking economics with psychology, sociology and health.

facts.text: It treats happiness and quality-of-life measures, rather than wealth, income or profit, as the thing to be maximised.
Happiness is measured with self-reported surveys and with objective measures such as lifespan, income and education.
Classical and neoclassical economics saw happiness as unmeasurable; happiness economics is described as a radical break with that tradition.
Once wealth reaches subsistence level, extra wealth adds much less to well-being.
Kahneman and Deaton (2010) found day-to-day emotional well-being rose with income only up to about $75,000 a year per household, though life satisfaction kept rising.
Direct happiness surveys are increasingly used as an alternative to GDP or GNP for judging policy success.
Critics worry that happiness metrics may serve political or even authoritarian goals, and that survey scales distort results through 'rounding'.

title: Easterlin paradox

definition.text: The Easterlin paradox is the finding that richer people in a country report more happiness than poorer ones, yet average happiness does not rise as the nation's average income grows.

facts.text: Richard Easterlin formulated it from survey results comparing happiness and GDP across and within countries.
There is a significant link between GDP and happiness across nations, which some researchers in 2002 said holds only up to about $15,000 GDP per person.
Several studies in the 2000s found the opposite, and more robust research links economic development with population well-being, so the paradox is disputed.

contested_note: Later studies have found a link between national income growth and happiness, so whether the paradox holds is disputed.

title: Human development (economics)

definition.text: Human development is a view of progress that widens economic development to include social, political and even ethical dimensions.

facts.text: The UN Development Programme defines it as enlarging people's choices to live a long healthy life, be educated, have a decent living standard and enjoy freedom and self-respect.
On this view economic growth is only a means of enlarging people's choices, not the goal itself.
The idea grew in the 1980s through Amartya Sen's capabilities perspective, with Mahbub ul Haq among its key early figures; the HDI stems from this work.
Aristotle already noted that wealth is merely useful for something else, not the good being sought.
Six pillars are listed: equity, sustainability, productivity, empowerment, cooperation and security.
UN Human Development Reports carry indices including the HDI, gender indices and a Human Poverty Index, later replaced by the Multidimensional Poverty Index.

title: OECD Better Life Index

definition.text: The OECD Better Life Index, launched in May 2011, is an OECD tool that measures several dimensions of economic and social progress beyond GDP.

facts.text: It grew out of the Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission's concern that GDP failed to give a true picture of people's current and future well-being.
It covers 11 topics of well-being, including housing, income, jobs, community, education and environment, each built from 1 to 4 measures.
Users rank each topic from 0 to 5 by importance to build their own index, and the OECD reports the pooled results in its How's Life? report.
Critics say its 11 dimensions miss things such as social networks and freedom of speech, and question its use of relative rather than absolute scores.

title: Social Progress Index

definition.text: The Social Progress Index, created by the Social Progress Imperative, measures the real-life outcomes people experience across many social and environmental indicators.

facts.text: Unlike other Beyond GDP measures, it deliberately leaves out all indicators of economic performance.
It defines social progress as meeting basic human needs, building blocks for better quality of life, and the chance for people to reach their full potential.
It was created in 2013 because its founders found the HDI and happiness indices insufficient.
Denmark and the United States have similar GDP per person, yet Denmark scores 10 points higher in social progress.

title: Sustainable national income

definition.text: Sustainable national income (SNI) estimates the highest production level at which, with that year's technology, vital environmental functions stay available for ever.

facts.text: Ordinary national income leaves out the loss of environmental functions, so it is always higher than the SNI.
The gap between national income and SNI shows how far production is from sustainability; a shrinking gap means progress, a growing one means drifting away.
Economist Roefie Hueting developed the framework, working with a multidisciplinary team at Statistics Netherlands for nearly forty years.
Following the precautionary principle, the SNI assumes no technological progress during the transition to sustainability.
Tinbergen and Hueting's rough 1991 world estimate put sustainable income at 50 percent of world production.
A 2001 estimate for the Netherlands also came to around 50 percent of national income, about the production level of the early 1970s.
Between 1990 and 2000 the Dutch gap between national income and SNI grew by about 10 billion euros.

title: Environmental functions

definition.text: Environmental functions are the possible uses of our non-human-made physical surroundings, on which people depend for producing, consuming, breathing and recreation.

facts.text: When one use comes at the expense of another, the functions compete; once water pollution passes a threshold, 'dumping ground for waste' competes with 'drinking water'.
Competing functions are scarce and so are economic goods; most functions that were once free goods have become scarce.

title: Adjusted net saving

definition.text: Adjusted net saving, or genuine savings, is ordinary net saving minus the value of resource depletion and environmental damage plus investment in human capital.

facts.text: It measures the net change in a nation's produced, natural and human capital stocks, valued in money.
It grew from Hartwick's rule, as Pearce, Atkinson and Hamilton set out a measure of net investment across kinds of capital.
A positive value is linked to the possibility of long-run sustainability, so policy should aim to keep it at or above zero.
The World Bank publishes these estimates for over 150 countries as 'adjusted savings' and suggests them as an alternative to GDP.
Along with ecological footprint accounts, it is an example of an index focused on overconsumption.
